prediction_ref.short_label: Multi-tenant agent builders draw a 9.0+ cross-tenant authz CVE by Q1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Today's lead is the precipitating origin signal and the class signature this thesis rests on. The Langflow cross-tenant IDOR fired in the wild is CVE-2026-55255, a CVSS 9.9 insecure-direct-object-reference (CWE-639) on a flow-execution endpoint: the get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name helper resolves a flow by UUID with no owner check, so any authenticated user can run another tenant's flow via /api/v1/responses. Sysdig's June 25 report is the first known in-the-wild exploitation, and the telemetry shows an operator harvesting flow IDs from GET /api/v1/flows/ then replaying them ~20 seconds later on POST /api/v1/responses with input 'leak api keys,' on an instance also running the KEV-listed RCE CVE-2026-33017. The structural read in today's reporting is exactly the prediction's premise: the soft underbelly of multi-tenant agent platforms is the orchestration and authorization plane -- opaque, harvestable flow/run/workspace IDs, a shared execution endpoint, and owner checks deferred to the UI rather than enforced server-side per object -- and the same architectural pattern recurs across the n8n / Flowise / Dify / LangGraph Platform / CrewAI peer class. The gap to the falsifiable bar: the prediction requires a SECOND, distinct named platform in this category (not Langflow) to receive a CVSS >= 9.0 advisory whose root cause is cross-tenant authorization, broken-object-level access, or IDOR, ideally with in-the-wild or CISA-KEV evidence. Today supplies the first instance and the structural trigger; the recurrence that would confirm the class has not yet landed.

prediction_ref.short_label: Major AI-agent platform ships zero-trust controls as default-on by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Today's two security advisories are the structural forcing function this defensive thesis is built around. The Langflow cross-tenant IDOR (CVE-2026-55255, CVSS 9.9) with first in-the-wild exploitation reported by Sysdig on June 25 proves the orchestration plane ships without deny-by-default per-tenant authorization: get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name resolved a flow by UUID with no owner check. The AutoGPT SSRF-protection bypass (CVE-2026-56663, CVSS 8.5, fixed in 0.6.52, published June 26) proves the execution plane ships without SSRF-hardened tool-call and egress defaults: the SendWebRequestBlock that agents use for outbound HTTP calls mishandles IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, re-opening the internal-IP filter so an agent can reach cloud metadata, internal admin panels, and databases. Together they make the prediction's exact case -- a fetch-arbitrary-URL block is by construction an SSRF surface, and a flow resolved by opaque ID is by construction a cross-tenant surface, unless authorization and egress are gated by default. The prediction's falsifiable target is at least one major AI-agent platform, orchestration vendor, or agentic IDE shipping zero-trust controls as default-on in a named release: deny-by-default per-tenant object-level authorization and/or default outbound-egress allowlisting with SSRF-hardened blocks. The gap to the bar: a blog post, an opt-in toggle, a one-off CVE patch, or a roadmap promise does not count -- and today supplies only the motivating CVEs, not a default-posture release.

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Today's two advisories are direct, in-the-wild evidence for the threat this default-deny thesis answers. The Langflow cross-tenant IDOR (CVE-2026-55255, CVSS 9.9) fired in the wild per Sysdig's June 25 report shows an agent-execution endpoint running another tenant's flow with no owner check, and the AutoGPT SSRF bypass (CVE-2026-56663, CVSS 8.5, fixed in 0.6.52) shows a general-purpose web-request block wired into agent workflows reaching internal services the agent was never meant to touch. Both are exactly the open-permission failure mode the prediction expects harnesses to close: a fetch-arbitrary-URL primitive and a broadly-scoped execution endpoint are dangerous precisely because the toolset and egress are allowed by default rather than gated. The prediction holds that coding-agent harnesses will make default-deny toolset gating the standard posture -- tools and network egress off until explicitly enabled per task. The gap to the bar: today supplies the motivating CVEs in agent platforms, not a harness shipping default-deny toolset gating as its standard. AutoGPT's own remediation is a one-off SSRF patch plus an operator instruction to constrain outbound egress, which is the manual version of the default the prediction expects to become standard -- not the default itself.
